rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening la refutes the claim that the Qur’an is soothsayer nonsense before affirming its truth; this abrupt denial is a natural, forceful rhetorical style.
rows.anchor: the objective is to negate some notion, view or objection of an addressee before affirming the real truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La should not be treated as superfluous: eloquent discourse has no superfluous words, and dismissing it without principle risks opening forbidden matters; Islahi will explain its Arabic usage at 57:29.
rows.anchor: there are no superfluous words in an eloquent discourse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawqiʿ means a place where something happens or falls; here the plural denotes the heavenly stations where jinn ambush divine secrets and are struck by meteors.
rows.anchor: the place where something happens or falls

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the Qur’an’s revelation God specially protected revelation from jinn eavesdroppers, who acknowledged that the sky’s stations were guarded by meteors.
rows.anchor: The jinn themselves have acknowledged this fact, as recorded in Sūrah Jinn thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s mawāqiʿ are their ambush stations, while this verse’s mawāqiʿ are the targets of the shooting stars; al-nujūm here means shooting stars.
rows.anchor: the first word refers to their ambuscade and the second to the targets of the shooting stars

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an elsewhere calls these meteors a bombardment against devils, and related explanations occur at 53:1–5 and 55:35.
rows.anchor: made them a means of bombardment on the devils

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is a parenthetical between oath and complement: reflection on the meteor barrier shows that devils cannot reach the divine realm as soothsayers claim, a great cosmic testimony whether people recognize it or not.
rows.anchor: This is a very apt parenthetical sentence between the object of the oath and the complement of the oath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath bears witness that the Qur’an is exalted revelation from God, kept in a protected book and accessible only to pure, near angels, never to jinn or devils.
rows.anchor: It is found in a protected book with the Almighty and no one except His pure angels can have access to it

rows.speaker: jurists
rows.claim: Jurists infer from the verse that ritual purity is required to touch or read the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: In their opinion, it is only in the state of this purity that a person is allowed to touch or read the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context gives this etiquette no direct bearing on the verse; requiring prayer-level purity to read or touch the Qur’an is excessive and an unbearable burden, obscuring its function as guidance and evidence.
rows.anchor: the view of those jurists who impose the same conditions of ritual purity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idhān means indifference, carelessness, or laziness; after describing the Qur’an’s exaltedness, God asks whether it deserves such treatment.
rows.anchor: means “to be indifferent, careless and lazy.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rejecters know the difference between a pebble and a pearl but dismiss the Qur’an as soothsayer speech; indifference cannot change reality, which they must face.
rows.anchor: they very well know the difference but do not want to accept the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word rizq is read as revelation and the Qur’an, God’s spiritual sustenance for eternal life; ancient scriptures and the Qur’an also use rizq for revelation.
rows.anchor: In ancient scriptures as well as in the Qur’an, divine revelation is called

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites Jesus’ teaching that spiritual life depends on every word from God, not bread alone.
rows.anchor: Man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supports revelation as spiritual nourishment by noting that the Qur’an calls its message life-giving.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān has also called divine revelation as life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death exposes human helplessness: if people imagine Qur’anic warning of judgment is a bluff and they answer to no one, they should save the dying or return the soul; death gathers all for God’s appointed day.
rows.anchor: why does not a person able to save himself or any of his near ones from the jaws of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “when it reaches the throat,” the subject “the soul” is suppressed but understood from context; the same ellipsis at 75:26 heightens the event’s horror through ambiguity.
rows.anchor: The subject of the verb is similarly suppressed in Sūrah Qiyāmah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even with family, well-wishers, and doctors present, the angel of death takes the soul before their eyes; their efforts cannot stop him, and God is nearer though unseen.
rows.anchor: before their very eyes, the angel of death claims his soul and no one can stop him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge in verses 86–87 answers the conditional begun in verse 85; the conditional is repeated because its answer was delayed.
rows.anchor: Since the conditional clause and its answer were distanced from one another, the conditional clause has been repeated here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madīn means subservient or under control.
rows.anchor: means “to be subservient and to be under control.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Death begins the real next phase, when humanity divides into three groups; for the favored, rawḥ means bliss and rayḥān ecstasy, though rayḥān literally means flower and also conveys sweet smell.
rows.anchor: it is also used in what it entails, ie. ecstasy and sweet smell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right-hand person receives God’s and the angels’ greeting; min explains the addressed pronoun rather than meaning “from,” so the sense is “O companion of the right hand, peace be for you.”
rows.anchor: O companion of the right hand! Peace be for you.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The left-hand group is labeled by its actual crime, rejection and misguidance, associating Quraysh’s fate with their denial; their first provision is boiling water, then Hell’s torment.
rows.anchor: they are addressed with reference to their real crime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The close assures the Prophet that the preceding realities are certain, urging patience and perseverance, leaving rejecters to themselves, and glorifying God as previously explained at verse 74.
rows.anchor: whatever has been mentioned earlier are certain facts. There is no possibility of any doubt in them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe glorifies God, and its glorification calls people to worship Him alone without associating partners.
rows.anchor: within this Universe is glorifying Him and this act of theirs invites mankind to worship Him only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims, especially the weak in faith, must honor their pledge to listen and obey by joining the Prophet’s call to fight and spend; this response brings them from darkness to light, and pre-conquest sacrifices rank higher though later ones are rewarded too.
rows.anchor: Those who today spend and fight in the way of God shall have a higher status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere spending becomes guiding light toward Paradise, while hypocrites who withhold it lose that light; when they seek to share the believers’ light, they are refused and a wall separates them from God’s blessings and leaves them with torment.
rows.anchor: Those who shall spend in the way of God with purity of purpose shall find that their spending has manifested itself into a radiant light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites who still hesitate and withhold spending despite Islam’s clear signs risk becoming hardhearted like the Jews; they are reminded that reckoning is certain.
rows.anchor: they shall become hardhearted like the Jews before them and meet a similar fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God greatly multiplies the reward for sincere spending and fighting, which qualifies people as ṣiddīqīn and shuhadā’ and earns them the radiant light denied to hypocrites.
rows.anchor: they shall be rewarded many times for each sacrifice they make

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section laments people’s timid investment in transient worldly pleasure, which makes them forget their Lord’s mercy and the Paradise as vast as heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: people who have given their hearts to the transitory pleasures of this world and have forgotten the mercy of their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and hardship follow divinely ordained destiny rather than personal schemes, so people should submit, spend when wealthy, and remember that God can give or take wealth.
rows.anchor: a person’s opulence or poverty does not depend on his own schemes and plans but on the fate which has been divinely ordained for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites who never truly entered Islam share the disbelievers’ fate in Hell; no one will hear their pleas, and their abode is evil.
rows.anchor: they will end with the same fate as the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section warns wavering hypocrites of Jewish-like hardheartedness, then encourages trust in God’s power to revive faith as He revives dead earth; spending is never a loss, earns seventyfold reward, and can lead to ṣiddīq and shuhadā’ ranks.
rows.anchor: God Who is able to enliven a dead piece of land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ephemeral worldly attractions make people forget the eternal kingdom, which is as wide as the heavens and earth and can be bought with the pebbles they have collected.
rows.anchor: which is as vast as the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since joy, grief, poverty, and affluence follow God’s destiny rather than one’s plans, the right response is gratitude in ease, patience in trials, and turning one’s heart to God.
rows.anchor: poverty and affluence, ease and difficulty of this world are not dependent on one’s schemes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although they claim faith, “those who have professed faith” here means the hypocrites under discussion, so they should reflect on faith’s obligations and fulfill them.
rows.anchor: refer to the hypocrites whose behaviour is under discussion here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs of the true call and its coming dominance are now clear; continuing doubts mean a person refuses Islam until every claim appears before his eyes, a faith God does not value, and persistent doubt can harden hearts like the Jews’ and lead to their sealing.
rows.anchor: unless they saw each and every claim it made should come true before their very eyes. Such a faith has no value before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Temporary doubts can affect sincere people without blame, but sheltering in doubt to silence inner calls of truth and excuse falsehood eventually strips a person of the ability to accept truth.
rows.anchor: if a person by seeking refuge in these doubts keeps lulling the calls of the truth which arise in him to sleep

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author begins to distinguish two aspects of the Qur’an by describing it as both reminder and truth.
rows.anchor: these two terms have been used to direct attention to two distinct

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s signs should have made hearts submit; Jews’ doubts persisted despite prophets and miracles, deprived them of Torah and most of the Qur’an, and the hypocrites risk the same doom through skepticism.
rows.anchor: the majority of them were deprived of the Qur’ ān as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dead-earth revival verse is well placed as a remedy for unbelief: without Hereafter belief, hypocrites see Qur’anic promises as deception and find sacrifice difficult; God points to observable resurrection signs and the Qur’an’s further proofs to strengthen courage for sacrifice.
rows.anchor: The real ailment which these hypocrites were afflicted with was that they did not have belief in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also addresses hypocrites’ intimidation by Islam’s numerically superior opponents and their doubt that Muslims can defeat Quraysh and make Mecca a center of Abraham’s call.
rows.anchor: these hypocrites were very over-awed by the grandeur of the opponents of Islam
